title: 2 Samuel 11:6–13
context: David summons Uriah from the front, asks about the war, and urges him to go home, hoping the pregnancy will be attributed to Uriah. Uriah refuses to go home while the ark, Israel and Judah are in tents and his comrades are in the field. Even when David makes him drunk, Uriah sleeps with the king’s servants. The narrative sets the foreign-born soldier’s integrity against the king’s deceit. Both traditions see Uriah’s faithfulness as an indictment of David and see in David’s maneuvering how one sin leads to the concealment of another.

verses.text: David sent to Joab, “Send me Uriah the Hittite.” Joab sent Uriah to David.
verses.arminianNotes:
David sends word to Joab to send Uriah the Hittite, and Joab sends him. The cover-up begins.

Arminian readers note that David responds to the consequence of sin not with repentance but with scheming, and that each further choice deepens his responsibility and hardens him in the path he has begun.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the king who once inquired of the LORD before acting (5:19, 23) now acts entirely through his own calculation, a sign of how sin dulls a believer’s dependence on God.

Both traditions see David’s summons as the first step in a plan to hide his sin, which only compounds it.

verses.text: When Uriah had come to him, David asked him how Joab did, and how the people fared, and how the war prospered.
verses.arminianNotes:
When Uriah arrives, David asks how Joab, the army and the war are doing. The questions are a pretext.

Arminian readers note the hollowness of David’s show of concern; he speaks of the welfare of the army while planning to deceive one of its most faithful soldiers, a warning about religious or public words used to cover private sin.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the Hebrew repeats the word for welfare or peace in David’s questions, which sharpens the irony that David is bringing anything but peace to Uriah. Many commentators point out the wordplay.

Both traditions read the conversation as a cover for deceit and see David’s duplicity as part of his sin.

verses.text: David said to Uriah, “Go down to your house and wash your feet.” Uriah departed out of the king’s house, and a gift from the king was sent after him.
verses.arminianNotes:
David tells Uriah to go home and wash his feet, and a gift from the king follows him. David wants Uriah to spend the night with his wife.

Arminian readers note that David’s apparent generosity is calculated manipulation, an attempt to make Uriah unknowingly cover for the king’s sin, and that gifts given to deceive add to guilt rather than lessen it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the invitation is generally understood as encouragement to go home, rest and be with his wife, so that the pregnancy would appear to be Uriah’s; David is using Uriah as an instrument of his concealment.

Both traditions see the gift as part of David’s deceit.

verses.text: But Uriah slept at the door of the king’s house with all the servants of his lord, and didn’t go down to his house.
verses.arminianNotes:
Uriah sleeps at the palace entrance with the king’s servants and does not go home. His refusal frustrates David’s plan.

Arminian readers note that Uriah freely chooses to stay with his fellow servants, and his integrity stands as a silent rebuke to the king who should have been the example of faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s providence frustrates David’s plan through the integrity of a faithful man, so that the attempt to hide sin begins to unravel; God does not allow his servant’s sin to stay concealed.

Both traditions see Uriah’s conduct as a striking contrast to David’s.

verses.text: When they had told David, saying, “Uriah didn’t go down to his house,” David said to Uriah, “Haven’t you come from a journey? Why didn’t you go down to your house?”
verses.arminianNotes:
When David learns Uriah did not go home, he asks why, since he has come from a journey. David presses his scheme.

Arminian readers note that David now has to argue openly for what he wants, and that persisting in a deceit after it has been resisted shows a will set on its course rather than turning back.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s question, seemingly concerned for Uriah’s comfort, masks his fear of exposure, and that sin makes people treat the integrity of others as an obstacle rather than an example.

Both traditions read David’s pressure as continued concealment and see in it a deepening of his guilt.

verses.text: Uriah said to David, “The ark, Israel, and Judah, are staying in tents; and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are encamped in the open field. Shall I then go into my house to eat and to drink, and to lie with my wife? As you live, and as your soul lives, I will not do this thing!”
verses.arminianNotes:
Uriah answers that the ark, Israel and Judah are in tents and his commander and comrades are in the field; how can he go home to eat, drink and lie with his wife? He swears by the king’s life he will not.

Arminian readers note that Uriah, a Hittite by origin, shows loyalty to God, king and comrades that David has abandoned, a reminder that faithfulness is measured by conduct, not by birth or office.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Uriah’s mention of the ark shows a reverence for the LORD’s presence with the army, and that soldiers on campaign customarily kept themselves from their wives (compare 1 Samuel 21:5).

Both traditions see Uriah’s words as an unintended but piercing indictment of David.

verses.text: David said to Uriah, “Stay here today also, and tomorrow I will let you depart.” So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day and the next day.
verses.arminianNotes:
David tells Uriah to stay one more day before returning, and Uriah stays in Jerusalem that day and the next. David buys time.

Arminian readers note that David is offered yet another moment in which he could stop and confess, and that God’s patience gives room for repentance even as the sinner persists in his own plans.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s extension of Uriah’s stay is a further maneuver, not a change of heart, and that the narrator lets the reader feel the tension as the king’s plan becomes more desperate.

Both traditions read the delay as part of David’s continued attempt to cover his sin rather than face it.

verses.text: When David had called him, he ate and drank before him; and he made him drunk. At evening, he went out to lie on his bed with the servants of his lord, but didn’t go down to his house.
verses.arminianNotes:
David invites Uriah to eat and drink and makes him drunk, but in the evening Uriah again sleeps with the servants and does not go home. Even drunk, Uriah keeps his word.

Arminian readers note the bitter irony that Uriah drunk is more faithful than David sober, and that David’s attempt to weaken another man’s resolve is itself a further sin.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David now uses wine to override Uriah’s conscience, compounding his guilt, while God, who governs all things, allows the scheme to fail so that the sin will come to light.

Both traditions see Uriah’s steadfastness as a rebuke to David and see David’s escalating schemes as the fruit of unconfessed sin.
